body:
HTTP/2 is a relatively new binary protocol rather than text-based.
There are a number of vectors that are possible, especially when downgrading is performed. These should be included here in the ASVS.

Some training material regarding this from PortSwigger Web Security Academy:
* [HTTP/2-exclusive vectors](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling/advanced/http2-exclusive-vectors)
* [HTTP/2 downgrading](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling/advanced/http2-downgrading)

I think 13.7.1 is not correctly worded. The formulation says:

> [ADDED] Verify **that the value** in the Content-Length request header field matches the calculated length using the built-in mechanism.

Here we are saying that we must verify that *value in a request* must match a given rule. This cannot be verified when there are untrusted clients. What we can verify if that the HTTP/2 server validates/enforces a correct `Content-Length`. We should formulate it as something like:

> [ADDED] Verify **that the HTTP/2 server validates** that the Content-Length request header field matches the calculated length using the built-in mechanism.

but I'm not sure that this formulation is that great either.

I think this applies to reverse proxy situation (HTTP/2+ to HTTP/1).

I think what we want to say is that if a Content-Length is provided in the upstream request, the reverse proxy must enforce the correct length in the downstream request (which may be difficult in some cases). Can we formulate it somewhat like that?

Does it make sense in other situations (outside of reverse proxy)?

Bonus question, wouldn't 13.7.1 apply to HTTP/1 as well, somehow?

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc2616#section-4.4

First some references from RFC 911x.

[Transfer Encoding](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#name-transfer-encoding) from RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1):

> A server MAY reject a request that contains both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding or process such a request in accordance with the Transfer-Encoding alone. <mark>Regardless, the server MUST close the connection after responding to such a request to avoid the potential attacks.</mark>

[Response Splitting](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#name-response-splitting) from RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1):

> Response splitting (a.k.a. CRLF injection) is a common technique, used in various attacks on Web usage, that exploits the line-based nature of HTTP message framing and the ordered association of requests to responses on persistent connections [[Klein](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#Klein)]. This technique can be particularly damaging when the requests pass through a shared cache.

[Malformed Messages](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#name-malformed-messages) from RFC 9113 (HTTP/2):

> Intermediaries that process HTTP requests or responses (i.e., any intermediary not acting as a tunnel) MUST NOT forward a malformed request or response. Malformed requests or responses that are detected MUST be treated as a [stream error](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#StreamErrorHandler) ([Section 5.4.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#StreamErrorHandler)) of type [PROTOCOL_ERROR](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#PROTOCOL_ERROR).

[HTTP Message Framing](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#name-http-message-framing) from 9114 (HTTP/3):

> Transfer codings (see [Section 7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7) of [[HTTP/1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9112)]) are not defined for HTTP/3; the Transfer-Encoding header field MUST NOT be used.

[Malformed Requests and Responses](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#name-malformed-requests-and-resp) from RFC 9114 (HTTP/3):

> A request or response that is defined as having content when it contains a Content-Length header field ([Section 8.6](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-8.6) of [[HTTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9110)]) is malformed if the value of the Content-Length header field does not equal the sum of the [DATA](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#frame-data) frame lengths received. A response that is defined as never having content, even when a Content-Length is present, can have a non-zero Content-Length header field even though no content is included in [DATA](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#frame-data) frames.
>
> Intermediaries that process HTTP requests or responses (i.e., any intermediary not acting as a tunnel) MUST NOT forward a malformed request or response. Malformed requests or responses that are detected MUST be treated as a [stream error](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#errors) of type [H3_MESSAGE_ERROR](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#H3_MESSAGE_ERROR).

***

Latest proposition for 13.7.1 was:

>  [ADDED] Verify that when downgrading from HTTP/2 to an older version, the standard mechanism for calculating request length is used. <mark>Ensure that conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding headers are not introduced</mark>, as they may lead to request smuggling vulnerabilities.

According to RFC 9112, Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding should not be used in the same HTTP/1.x request anyway. We could simplify the seconde part of proposed 13.7.1 as.

> Verify that intermediaries (such as reverse proxies) do not include both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding when emitting HTTP/1.x messages, for example when downgrading from HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 to HTTP/1.x.

→ This part would *not* be in the HTTP/1 section.

The first part of proposed 13.7.1 might be replaced by:

> Verify that when a content-length header field is present in a HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 message defined as having content, the message is rejected if the body length is different from the length advertised in the content-length header field.

***

Proposed 13.7.2, I would include HTTP/3 as per the section of RFC 9114 quoted above:

> [ADDED] Verify that all Transfer-Encoding header fields are stripped from HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 messages or that HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 *messages* containing them are rejected entirely to prevent response splitting and header injection attacks.

Note: changed "HTTP/2 requests" to "HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 *messages*"

***

Proposed 13.7.3 (CRLF in HTTP/2) appears to be related to the [Response Splitting](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112.html#name-response-splitting) of RFC 9112 (about HTTP/1.1).

I would reformulate as:

> [ADDED] Verify that any full CRLF (\r\n) sequence within a HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 header *fields* is either removed or rejected to prevent header injection attacks.

Note: changed "HTTP/2 header" into "HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 header *fields*" (because in HTTP/2 the header is binary anyway so what we really care about is whether there is a CRLF in a header field?).

In addition, I am wondering if a requirement would be needed for this snippet of RFC 9112 (HTTP/1.1):

> A server MAY reject a request that contains both Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding or process such a request in accordance with the Transfer-Encoding alone.Regardless, the server MUST close the connection after responding to such a request to avoid the potential attacks.

Ensure that conflicting Content-Length and Transfer-Encoding header **fields** are not introduced, as they may lead to request smuggling vulnerabilities. |
| **13.7.2** | [ADDED] Verify that all Transfer-Encoding header fields are stripped from HTTP/2 messages or that HTTP/2 requests containing them are rejected ~~entirely~~ to prevent response splitting and header injection attacks. |
| **13.7.3** | [ADDED] Verify that any full CRLF (\r\n) sequence within a HTTP/2 header is either removed or rejected to prevent header injection attacks. |

> What is the difference between 4.2.1 and 4.3.1?

I think that the intent of 4.2.1 is to say, that when you are *receiving* a message with `Transfer-Encoding` (in HTTP/1.x), you must disregard `Content-Length` for the intent of deciding where the incoming message ends (and where the next one begins). This applies to clients, servers and (reverse) proxies.

I think that the intent of the first sentence of 4.3.1 is to day the same thing for HTTP/2. In HTTP/2, there is no  `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` so 4.2.1 as currently formulated does not apply. Instead the end of the message is signaled by the `END_STREAM` flag. When processing a HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3) message, the receiver must ignore `Content-Length` for determining the 

Maybe these two can be merged into a single one?

I think that the second sentence of 4.3.1 is intended to make sure that the reverse proxy does not generate a *HTTP/1.x* message containing both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` HTTP header fields:

* I think this should better be a separate requirement from the first sentence of 4.3.1.
* I think it could be generalized as "never send a *HTTP/1.x* message containing both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding` (when acting as a reverse proxy and otherwise).

***

> If 4.3.1 is satisified (Transfer-Encoding header fields are stripped or that HTTP/2 requests containing them are rejected) how the other are still relevant? 

I'm not sure. I think 4.3.2 as I stands is not very clear which makes answering your question not easy :)

One problem with 4.3.2 is that it mixes a requirement about HTTP message and HTTP requests:

> Verify that all Transfer-Encoding header fields are stripped from HTTP/2 **messages** or that HTTP/2 **requests** containing them are rejected to prevent response splitting and header injection attacks.

The first part of the sentence is a requirement about HTTP/2 messages (requests and responses) while the second part if about requests only.

I think the intent of this requirement is (or should be) to make sure than the sender does not generate a HTTP/2 message with a `Transfer-Encoding` header field:

* because it is `Transfer-Encoding` header field is forbidden in HTTP/2;
* and because this would confuse the receiver of the message and trigger some HTTP smuggling attack.

In this case, this might be merged into the second sentence of 4.3.1 (which should be separated from the first sentence of 4.3.1).

> I feel like that generation of an HTTP/1 request outside of the context of downgrading seems very niche indeed. Do you really think it is worth getting into that here?

I would say that the current 4.3.1 ("when downgrading from HTTP/2 to an older HTTP version") is quite niche already as it  is usually implemented by reverse proxy only and usually not by application code i.e. you need to make sure that NGINX and friends are OK in this regard but that's basically it (outside things like [ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/)).

Some case where it might make sense (for HTTP/1, HTTP/2 or HTTP/3) is when the a malicious actor would be able to set a `Content-Length` header in a HTTP request sent by the the application.

> In general, it feels like the wording has gotten a lot more complicated. 

Oh yes, it needs simplification.

> Could we not simplify it to: "Verify that when downgrading messages to HTTP/1, the Content-Length header field does not conflicting with the length of the content as determined by the framing of the HTTP protocol, in order to prevent request smuggling attacks."?

What about something such as (with the intent of still covering the "not downgrading" case):

> Verify that when generating messages, the Content-Length header field does not conflict with the length of the content as determined by the framing of the HTTP protocol, in order to prevent request smuggling attacks.

***

> "Verify that Transfer-Encoding header fields are stripped from HTTP/2 requests or that requests containing them are rejected to prevent response splitting (and header injection attacks. [ed note: if we decide this is correct])"

The intent of my proposition was to focus on *generating/sending* HTTP messages instead of *receiving/downgrading* them. The proposed wording is somewhat consistent with RFC 9113 and RFC 9114:

> An endpoint MUST NOT generate an HTTP/2 message containing connection-specific header fields. […] Any message containing connection-specific header fields MUST be treated as [malformed](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#malformed) ([Section 8.1.1](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9113#malformed)).

> An endpoint MUST NOT generate an HTTP/3 field section containing connection-specific fields; any message containing connection-specific fields MUST be treated as [malformed](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9114#malformed).

But actually these snippets are actually saying both:

* you shall not generate such as message;
* and you shall reject such an incoming message.

So maybe 4.3.2 should cover both:

> Verify that the application does not send nor accept HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 messages with connection-specific header fields such as Transfer-Encoding to prevent response splitting and header injection attacks.
